_: Reference tables for the regions block: typical impacts of a strong eastern-type El Niño by region and season, food-import vulnerability, and what to do. Every row carries a source; a row without one must not reach the panel. Impacts are TYPICAL, not guaranteed: the panel says 'usually', never 'will'. Strength: robust (appears in most strong events) / likely (majority) / weak (some, or contested in the literature). Vulnerability 1–5: share of imports in cereal consumption and exposure of food-insecure populations, from FAO/World Bank reports.

season_notes.SON: September-October-November. The season when El Niño is building towards its peak: the teleconnections are already switched on, and in the southern hemisphere it is the planting season.
season_notes.DJF: December-January-February. The peak season of almost every El Niño and the strongest teleconnections: the southern African and Australian summer, the northern winter.
season_notes.MAM: March-April-May. The decaying phase: the ocean is still warm, and the food consequences of the peak season arrive as harvests and prices.

sources.cpc: NOAA CPC, El Niño and La Niña: typical global impacts (warm-episode maps, DJF and JJA), cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/analysis_monitoring/impacts
sources.iri: IRI, ENSO impacts by region and season, iri.columbia.edu/our-expertise/climate/enso
sources.giews: FAO GIEWS Special Alert 373, El Niño 2023–24: potential impacts on food security (Aug 2023)
sources.wfp: WFP, El Niño 2023–24 anticipatory action plans and regional outlooks
sources.nfidc: FAO / WTO list of Net Food-Importing Developing Countries; FAO cereal import dependency ratios (FAOSTAT food balances)
sources.wb: World Bank, Food Security Update (2024–2025), country import dependence
sources.ep: Eastern-Pacific (canonical) type: Rasmusson & Carpenter 1982; Ashok et al. 2007; coastal Peru impacts, SENAMHI/ENFEN bulletins
sources.euro: Brönnimann 2007, Impact of El Niño–Southern Oscillation on European climate, Reviews of Geophysics 45; Ineson & Scaife 2009, the stratospheric pathway to late-winter Europe, Nature Geoscience 2
sources.arabia: Winter (Nov–Mar) rainfall of the Arabian Peninsula and the Gulf responds to ENSO through the subtropical jet: Kumar et al., ENSO influence on Arabian Peninsula winter rainfall; NOAA CPC seasonal outlooks for Southwest Asia
sources.gcc: Gulf food security: FAO/World Bank country briefs — the GCC imports 80–90 % of its food; national strategies (UAE National Food Security Strategy 2051, Saudi General Food Security Authority)
sources.eurasia: ENSO signal over Russia and Central Asia is weak and season-dependent: Brönnimann 2007; NOAA CPC composite maps; Central Asian winter-spring precipitation response documented in regional studies (Barlow et al.)

actions.drought: Pre-position drought-tolerant seed and fodder, plan water rationing, protect livestock, contract grain imports early.
actions.flood: Flood preparedness: drainage, protect stored grain, health measures for water-borne disease, early warning for river basins.
actions.heat: Heat plans for cities and crops, irrigation scheduling, protection of vulnerable groups.
actions.import: Forward-contract cereal imports, build strategic reserves, budget for price rises, target social safety nets.
actions.fisheries: Prepare for a collapse of coastal upwelling fisheries: fishing bans, income support, alternative supply of fish protein.
actions.watch: No strong local signal: watch the harvests of the exporters you buy from and the world price, not the local sky.
actions.none: No strong signal: watch the neighbours' harvests and world prices rather than local weather.

regions.name: East Africa
regions.countries: Kenya, Somalia, southern Ethiopia, Tanzania, Uganda

SON.note: Short rains (Oct–Dec) usually well above normal; flooding and landslides, and conditions that favour desert locust breeding.

DJF.note: The wet tail of the short rains runs into January; standing water and disease follow.

MAM.note: The long rains show no consistent El Niño signal.

vulnerability.note: Large food-insecure population; cereal imports are 20–40 % of consumption in Kenya and Somalia; floods hit pastoral and lowland cropping areas hardest.

regions.name: Southern Africa
regions.countries: Zimbabwe, Zambia, Malawi, Mozambique, South Africa, Botswana, Namibia

SON.note: A late and weak start of the rainy season delays planting.

DJF.note: The main maize season runs drier and hotter than normal: 1982-83, 1991-92, 2015-16 and 2023-24 all brought regional maize failures.

MAM.note: Rains end early and the harvest is cut short.

vulnerability.note: Maize-dependent diets and thin reserves; Zimbabwe, Malawi and Zambia declared drought emergencies in 2024.

SON.note: No consistent signal for the second rainy season.

MAM.note: A weak and mixed signal at the start of the first rainy season.

vulnerability.note: Rice and wheat imports matter (Nigeria, Ghana); the exposure runs through world prices rather than local weather.

regions.name: Sahel
regions.countries: Mali, Niger, Chad, Burkina Faso, Senegal, Sudan

SON.note: The rainy season (Jul–Sep) tends to be weaker in El Niño years; by September it is mostly over, so the effect is already in the standing crop.

vulnerability.note: The highest structural food insecurity, conflict, and cereal imports of 30–60 % of consumption in Mauritania and Senegal; any price shock becomes a crisis.

regions.name: Gulf and Arabian Peninsula
regions.countries: UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain, Yemen

SON.note: The winter rain season has not started; no consistent signal.

DJF.note: El Niño strengthens the subtropical jet over Arabia, and winter rainfall runs above normal: the documented pathway behind heavy-rain and flash-flood episodes on the peninsula, including the April 2024 Gulf floods.

MAM.note: The wet tendency fades through spring; heat arrives early.

vulnerability.note: The Gulf states import 80–90 % of their food and grow almost no cereals: the exposure is entirely to world prices, shipping and the harvests of exporters. Yemen combines that dependence with an ongoing food emergency.

regions.name: North Africa and the Levant
regions.countries: Egypt, Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Iran

SON.note: No consistent signal at the start of the wet season.

DJF.note: The eastern Mediterranean and Iraq–Iran tend to be wetter; north-west Africa shows a mixed and weaker response.

MAM.note: No consistent signal; local drought there is driven more by the Atlantic than by the Pacific.

vulnerability.note: The world's largest wheat importers: Egypt, Algeria and Morocco import 50–75 % of their cereals, and Lebanon and Jordan more. Exposure runs through world prices and the harvests of the Black Sea exporters.

SON.note: Autumn shows no reliable El Niño signal over Europe.

DJF.note: Early winter is dominated by the North Atlantic, not the Pacific: the El Niño signal is weak and inconsistent between events.

MAM.note: Late winter and early spring carry the clearest, still weak, signal: a stratospheric pathway that tends towards a negative North Atlantic Oscillation, which usually means colder and drier northern Europe and wetter southern Europe and the Mediterranean.

vulnerability.note: A net exporter of cereals overall and wealthy enough to outbid others on the world market; the risk here is price, not availability. A poor southern-European harvest raises world prices for the importers elsewhere.

regions.name: Russia and Central Asia
regions.countries: European Russia, Siberia, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan

SON.note: No reliable signal for the autumn sowing of winter wheat.

DJF.note: Winters in European Russia tend to be milder in El Niño years, but the effect is small next to the Atlantic and Arctic drivers and does not repeat reliably.

MAM.note: Central Asia (Kazakhstan to Tajikistan) tends towards a wetter winter and spring, which is favourable for the grain crop; for Russia itself the spring signal is not distinguishable from noise.

vulnerability.note: Russia and Kazakhstan are among the largest wheat exporters: what matters for the world is their harvest, not their imports. A poor Black Sea crop is the single fastest route from weather to global bread prices.

regions.name: South Asia
regions.countries: India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal

SON.note: The monsoon withdraws earlier; the north-east monsoon is mixed, and southern India and Sri Lanka are often wetter.

DJF.note: A warmer and drier winter in northern India and Pakistan; the rabi wheat crop is exposed to March heat.

MAM.note: Pre-monsoon heat waves become more likely.

vulnerability.note: Largely self-sufficient in cereals but with a huge population close to the margin; India restricts exports in bad years, and that alone moves world rice prices.

regions.name: Southeast Asia and Indonesia
regions.countries: Indonesia, Philippines, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, Papua New Guinea

SON.note: A delayed monsoon onset, drought and peat fires in Indonesia and Malaysia; the Philippines run dry.

DJF.note: Reduced rainfall persists; rice and palm-oil yields fall and Philippine drought deepens.

MAM.note: A dry tail: reservoirs low, hydropower reduced.

vulnerability.note: Rice self-sufficiency is thin in Indonesia and the Philippines, and both import in El Niño years; Thailand and Vietnam are exporters whose smaller crops raise world prices.

SON.note: Southern China is somewhat wetter in autumn.

DJF.note: A wetter winter in southern China and a milder winter in Japan and Korea.

MAM.note: A wetter spring in south China; the following summer often brings Yangtze flooding, as in 1998 and 2016.

vulnerability.note: China holds large reserves but is the largest soybean and a major maize importer; Japan and Korea import most of their cereals but are wealthy enough to secure them.

regions.name: Australia and New Zealand
regions.countries: eastern and northern Australia, New Zealand

SON.note: Spring is drier and hotter in the east and north; the winter crop finishes badly and the bushfire season starts early.

DJF.note: A hot, dry summer in the east, bushfires, and a delayed northern wet season.

vulnerability.note: A major wheat exporter: a poor Australian crop tightens the world wheat balance and raises prices for importers elsewhere.

regions.name: Pacific Islands
regions.countries: Fiji, Papua New Guinea highlands, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Tuvalu, Micronesia

SON.note: The western Pacific (PNG, Fiji, Vanuatu) runs dry while the central Pacific (Kiribati, Tuvalu) is much wetter; sea level drops in the west and exposes reefs.

DJF.note: Drought in the west persists, and tropical cyclone activity shifts east towards French Polynesia and the Cooks.

vulnerability.note: Small islands import most staples and depend on shipping; the 1997-98 event brought famine conditions to the PNG highlands.

SON.note: Weak autumn signals; the Atlantic hurricane season is usually suppressed.

DJF.note: The southern tier from California to Florida runs wetter, the northern US and Canada warmer and drier; the Pacific North-west and the Ohio valley run dry.

MAM.note: A wet spring in the southern Plains and the Gulf, which is good for winter wheat.

vulnerability.note: The largest maize and soybean exporter; El Niño winters are usually favourable for US crops, which eases world supply.

regions.name: Central America and the Caribbean
regions.countries: Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Haiti, Cuba, Dominican Republic

SON.note: The dry corridor (Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua) runs dry and the second bean and maize crop is at risk.

DJF.note: The Caribbean is drier than normal.

MAM.note: A late start of the first rainy season.

vulnerability.note: Haiti and the dry-corridor countries combine high import dependence with chronic food insecurity and out-migration.

SON.note: Coastal Ecuador and northern Peru begin to see heavy rain; the coastal El Niño effect is strongest in eastern-type events.

DJF.note: Torrential rain and floods on the Peruvian and Ecuadorian coast, as in 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2017; the anchoveta fishery collapses while the Bolivian altiplano and the southern Peruvian Andes run dry.

MAM.note: Coastal floods persist through the southern autumn, with landslides and disease outbreaks.

vulnerability.note: Peru imports wheat and maize; fishmeal exports and coastal agriculture (rice, mango, asparagus) are hit directly, and Colombia and Bolivia rely on imported wheat.

regions.name: Southern Cone
regions.countries: southern Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay, northern Argentina; north-east Brazil

SON.note: Southern Brazil, Uruguay and north-east Argentina run wetter, with floods in the Paraná basin, while north-east Brazil runs dry.

DJF.note: A wet summer favourable for Argentine soybean and maize once the floods drain; north-east Brazil stays in drought.

MAM.note: A wet autumn delays the harvest.

vulnerability.note: Net exporters of soybean, maize and wheat: the world-price effect is usually favourable because the crops are bigger, and the local risk is floods and the north-eastern drought.
